clue.text: 20 submarine base reported to be totally secure

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by the spoken sound of the next words

parts.note: totally is wholly and to secure is to lock

explanation.surface: Someone vouches that a naval submarine base is completely safe from intruders.
explanation.walkthrough: 20-across is SCOTTISH. Holy Loch on the Firth of Clyde was a US Navy Polaris submarine base from 1961 to 1992; a loch is a Scottish lake or sea inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy Loch in Argyll housed American nuclear submarines through the Cold War, making it a famous naval base in Scotland.

clue.text: Amerind procreates without benefit of pastor

indicators.note: doing without something means going without it, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these six letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: A Native American has children without a church wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike P, A, S, T, O and one R from PROCREATES, wherever they fall, and C, R, E, E remain in order.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cree are a First Nations people of Canada, and Amerind is an older term for an indigenous American person.

clue.text: Umpire? He was out at the cinema

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the one with the casting vote who decides between two sides

definitions.text: He was out at the cinema
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the hero of Carol Reed's 1947 film ... Out

explanation.walkthrough: The second half needs the film title completed: the figure who was 'Out' in the cinema is the title's man.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter holding the deciding vote among an even number of judges is traditionally called the odd man, which is an umpire's role.

clue.text: Rider covers awfully nice first long drawers

indicators.note: one thing covering others wraps around them on both sides

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is an addition or rider tacked onto a letter

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the word is mangled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the word after it

parts.note: the opening letter of long

explanation.surface: A horse rider wears pretty long underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: A rider is an addition to a document, as a postscript is to a letter. 'Drawers' looks like underwear but means things that draw.
explanation.definitionFit: Pencils are writing and sketching tools, so they are literally things used for drawing pictures.

clue.text: See 20
Symbolic of Japan? Quite the reverse at the end of the day

definitions.text: Symbolic of Japan? Quite the reverse at the end of the day

parts.words: Symbolic of Japan? Quite the reverse
parts.note: surface reading: something representing Japan, then its opposite

parts.words: at the end of the day
parts.note: setter's reading: Japan is the land of the rising sun, and the opposite of rising is what the sun does at dusk

explanation.surface: A puzzle about national symbols ends with a weary 'at the end of the day'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' sounds like a cliché but is literal: evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Japan's flag shows a rising sun; the opposite image is the sun going down in the evening, literally the close of day.

clue.text: 20 smackers? Utter transport!

indicators.note: to utter is to say out loud, so we want the spoken sound of the next word

parts.note: buses are public road transport; the kissing word is spelt with a double S

explanation.surface: An exclamation of disgust at transport, as if shouting 'utter rubbish!'
explanation.walkthrough: A buss is an old word, kept in Scots, for a hearty kiss; a smacker is slang for a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: A smacker is a loud kiss, and busses are kisses in old English and Scots usage.

clue.text: Jail-bait?

parts.note: surface reading: an under-age person who could land someone in jail
setter's reading: bait is food, so prison food; the dish also names a prison sentence in British slang

explanation.walkthrough: Doing porridge is British slang for serving time in prison, and porridge is the classic Scottish breakfast, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal gruel was standard prison breakfast, so the dish became slang for a jail term; bait here means a meal.

clue.text: A rendezvous at Shaftesbury

definitions.note: the answer completes the London street name Shaftesbury Avenue

parts.note: taken as written
a rendezvous is a meeting place

explanation.surface: An arrangement to meet someone in London's West End theatre district.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaftesbury Avenue is the London street lined with West End theatres.
explanation.definitionFit: The full street name is Shaftesbury Avenue, so the missing second word is what the single word stands in for.

clue.text: Nice, so they say, stretch of 20 water

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so we use the sound

parts.note: nice means pleasant or good

explanation.surface: Someone praises a pleasant stretch of water in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Fyne is a long sea loch in Argyll, famous for its kippers and oysters; 'Nice' might suggest the French city.
explanation.definitionFit: Loch Fyne is a sea inlet on Scotland's west coast, a long body of salt water reaching inland.

clue.text: See 15
It holds one up at last

definitions.text: It holds one up at last

parts.words: It holds one up at last
parts.note: surface reading: something that finally supports a person, or a delay

parts.words: It holds one up at last
parts.note: setter's reading: when one's time is up at the very end, this box contains one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' means finished, as in 'time's up'; 'holds' means contains, not supports.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffin is the box a dead person is placed in, holding them when their life has ended.

clue.text: It's to be cast by the sinless Matthew and Mark on being consumed by fervour

definitions.text: It's to be cast by the sinless

indicators.note: what is consumed is taken inside, so the words before go into the next one

parts.note: fire is passion or fervour
Saint Matthew, abbreviated ST
Saint Mark, abbreviated ST
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sermon on the Gospels: Matthew and Mark preached with fervour about the sinless.
explanation.walkthrough: Gospel writers are saints, so each name stands for the abbreviation of Saint.
explanation.definitionFit: In John's Gospel Jesus says let him who is without sin cast the first stone, so the sinless one throws it.

clue.text: A Bolshevik leaning over to include a number back

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a ship that lists leans over to one side

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: nine is a number

explanation.surface: A Bolshevik tilts back to fit in one more number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaning over' looks like part of the surface picture, but it is the word for a ship tilting.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Lenin, leader of the Bolshevik faction that seized power in Russia in 1917, is a Bolshevik.

clue.text: After tea Leslie came inside, returning with family rubbish for 20 architect

parts.note: char is British slang for tea
Les is the short form of Leslie

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the two words before are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
inner means on the inside
kin are one's family
tosh is nonsense

explanation.surface: Leslie came indoors after tea and went back out with the family's rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came inside' looks like a phrase about Leslie, but the two words are separate pieces turned round together to give two of the architect's names.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Rennie Mackintosh was the Glasgow designer of the School of Art, the leading Scottish architect of Art Nouveau.

clue.text: Terms of article written in a fit of spite

indicators.note: something written in is placed inside, so one piece goes within the other
a fit is a convulsion, which throws the letters into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the definite article

explanation.surface: Insulting words chosen for an article written in a spiteful rage.
explanation.definitionFit: Epithets are descriptive names or labels, often abusive ones, so they are words or terms applied to a person.

clue.text: 20 city, working gas in radiance

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the second

parts.note: a glow is a soft radiance

indicators.note: letters that are working are moving about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A Scottish city lit by gas lamps working in a warm radiance.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow is the largest city in Scotland, on the River Clyde.

clue.text: Statistician has lost the bill, old boy! I first give notice of being late

indicators.note: losing something leaves it out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
taken as written; the next word places it at the front, right after the former pupil
an actuary is a statistician who calculates insurance risks
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: An exasperated note: the statistician has lost the bill, and I must apologise for being late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being late' looks like tardiness, but late here means dead.
explanation.definitionFit: An obituary is a published announcement of someone's death, and the late are those recently deceased.

clue.text: The opposite of that let out? It's a prickly one

parts.note: this is the counterpart of that

indicators.note: out means out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about opposites, then a remark about a prickly character.
explanation.walkthrough: The thistle is the national emblem of Scotland, fitting the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A thistle is a plant with sharp spiny leaves, so it is a prickly specimen of flora.

clue.text: This cast no blight on semi-conventional party

indicators.note: something blighted is spoiled and ruined, so these letters are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: semi means half, so only half the word is kept and the rest dropped

parts.note: taken as written; its back half is kept

explanation.surface: A cast of actors casts no shadow over a fairly conventional party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters; 'blight' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish National Party, the SNP, is the political party campaigning for Scottish independence.

clue.text: Keep talking about the setting of the Ring

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ..., carry on chatting
second meaning: the bezel or setting that holds a ring's stone

explanation.surface: Someone keeps talking about where Wagner's Ring cycle is set.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes 'Ring' look like Wagner's opera cycle; it is just a finger ring.
explanation.definitionFit: To chat on is to continue conversing, and a chaton is the jeweller's term for the mount holding a ring's gem.

clue.text: See 15
Modes of loads of Toad's odes

definitions.text: Modes of loads of Toad's odes

parts.words: Modes of loads of Toad's odes
parts.note: surface reading: the styles of Mr Toad's many boastful poems from The Wind in the Willows

parts.words: Modes of loads of Toad's odes
parts.note: setter's reading: modes, loads, Toad's and odes all share an ending sound, so the clue is an example of its own answer

explanation.walkthrough: Mr Toad in The Wind in the Willows composes conceited songs about himself; the clue's four sound-alike words show what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: Words with matching end sounds, like modes and odes, are rhymes, the stock device of comic verse.

clue.text: Drunken kilty whams a dram …

indicators.note: a drunken person staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A drunk man in a kilt knocks back a dram.
explanation.walkthrough: A kilty is a kilt-wearer, a Scotsman; a dram is a small measure of whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A dram is a measure of spirits, usually Scotch, and malt whisky is the classic drink poured as one.

clue.text: … and another, by the sound of it, on a 20 isle, while …

indicators.note: going by sound means we hear the word rather than see its spelling

parts.note: following the previous clue's dram, another drink: rum

explanation.surface: Continuing the drinking: one more dram on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhum (now usually spelt Rum) is one of the Small Isles of the Inner Hebrides; the ellipses chain this clue to 23 and 25.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhum is an island of the Inner Hebrides off Scotland's west coast, so it is a Scottish isle.

clue.text: A piece of fleece

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a chess piece, the castle
second meaning: to swindle or cheat someone of money

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a scrap of sheep's wool; both words have other senses.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the castle is called a rook, and to rook a person is to overcharge or swindle them, like fleecing.

clue.text: 20 cap some vermouth (not of the French)

indicators.note: not here means without, so the following words are left out

parts.note: Dubonnet is a brand of fortified wine aperitif, a vermouth-like drink
du is French for of the

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's cap is soaked in vermouth, though not the French kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not of the French' seems to rule out French vermouth, but it removes the French word du.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonnet is the traditional soft woollen cap worn by Scotsmen, as in the Balmoral or tam o' shanter.

clue.text: It controls drift when Rosie's apathetic, they say

indicators.note: what they say is spoken, so we listen to the sound

parts.note: Rosie Lee, Cockney rhyming slang for tea, gives the surname; apathetic means bored

explanation.surface: A boat drifts aimlessly because Rosie can't be bothered to steer.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosie Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, so Rosie's surname is Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: A leeboard is a plank lowered on a boat's side to stop it being pushed sideways by the wind, so it resists drift.
